summary:
Chhattisgarh stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Within Chhattisgarh, the recorded lethal violence against a trans person is a contract killing. On 22 November 2024 the Times of India reported that Kajal, alias "Coca Cola", a transgender woman, was lured out, stabbed and dumped in an abandoned quarry at village Dhabadih in Baloda Bazar district. The killing was ordered by a rival, Tapasya, for Rs 12 lakh to block Kajal's ascent to the Jora Math community head seat, the guru gaddi. Five suspects were arrested and Rs 10.5 lakh seized.

Festival entry in Bastar district has been screened on religious grounds. The Times of India reported on 23 September 2025 that the VHP and Bajrang Dal objected to non-Hindu sponsors of Navratri garba events and claimed the events had become platforms of obscenity and vulgarity, with participants admitted only if a tilak was applied. Non-Hindu participation in public cultural events is contested by Hindu nationalist groups, and the resulting conditions are imposed on whoever presents at the gate.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints, in police contact and at gated public events rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, and a trans woman was murdered in Chhattisgarh in November 2024, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The Bastar garba screening is a religion test, not a gender test. Organisers applied a tilak to entrants and Hindu nationalist groups policed sponsorship and conduct; gender-nonconforming visitors are not the stated target, but a gate that examines and marks each entrant puts them in front of actors with no stake in their privacy. The same outing mechanism appears at festival screening in Maharashtra, there combined with Aadhaar document checks that are absent from the Chhattisgarh events.

Festival exposure is seasonal and driven by community organisers at private-adjacent events, so it clusters around Navratri rather than operating year-round. Reported objections in Bastar led to at least three garba nights being called off with tickets cancelled, and police received a memorandum and arranged venue security, which lowers the likelihood of confrontation at the gate itself.

The Kajal killing was intra-community: the stated motive was succession to the guru gaddi at Jora Math, not anti-trans animus by outsiders. It nonetheless shows that a trans woman's public standing and mobility can be targeted through contract violence, and that the risk ran through the community's own hierarchy rather than through street hostility.

Criminal-law protection across India weakened in 2024 with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and Chhattisgarh shares that code. Against it, the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police and repeated high-court intervention remain available, and the UK Home Office's December 2025 country note describes police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and not systemic, though likelier in conservative rural areas.

Trans community governance in Chhattisgarh runs through the guru gaddi, the community head seat. In November 2024 a rival, Tapasya, allegedly commissioned the killing of Kajal, alias "Coca Cola", to stop her taking the Jora Math seat; five suspects were arrested and Rs 10.5 lakh of the Rs 12 lakh payment was seized. Residents navigating succession within these structures face a documented precedent of lethal competition.

Local police in Baloda Bazar district handled the Dhabadih quarry investigation and made the arrests within days of the 22 November 2024 report. In Bastar district, organisers responded to written objections from the VHP and Bajrang Dal by imposing religion-gated entry conditions on Navratri garba events, and police took a memorandum and provided venue security, which is the channel residents used to contest or accept those conditions.

Welfare-scheme access for residents turns on the national recognition test, which since March 2026 is limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary residents who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the scheme, regardless of how they are treated locally.
outOfScopeNotes:
Chhattisgarh-specific implementation of the March 2026 national amendment is not sourced here: no state-level recognition procedure, district-level documentation practice or welfare-office guidance for Chhattisgarh appears in the inventory, so how the narrowed test is applied at Raipur or district offices remains unresolved.

No Chhattisgarh High Court ruling on gender recognition, police conduct toward trans people, or the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita's effect on trans complainants is available in the inventory. Whether the removal of gender-identity-specific offences in 2024 has changed charging practice in Chhattisgarh is not sourced.

The outcome of the Kajal case is unresolved: five suspects were arrested and Rs 10.5 lakh seized as of 22 November 2024, but no charge-sheet, trial or conviction is recorded. Whether Tapasya was among those arrested is not stated in the source.

Whether religion-gated entry conditions of the Bastar type are applied at garba or other festivals elsewhere in Chhattisgarh is not sourced; the inventory covers one district and one festival season. The claim that such gates out gender-nonconforming visitors is an inference from the screening mechanism, not a reported incident.

No Chhattisgarh-specific data on police abuse of LGBT+ people exists in the inventory; the UK Home Office country note of December 2025 is national and does not disaggregate by state.
